claims.text: What the image looks like Solid hypoechoic thyroid nodule, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide, irregular margins → thyroid malignancy risk (TI-RADS 4-5)
claims.quote: Solid hypoechoic thyroid nodule, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide, irregular margins Thyroid malignancy risk (TI-RADS 4-5)

claims.quote: This ultrasound scan shows a nodule in the left thyroid lobe. The nodule is 51 millimeters across on the longitudinal axis and 31 millimeters on the anteroposterior axis.

claims.quote: Hypoechoic (dark gray) = complex fluid, abscess, solid hypoechoic mass.

claims.text: Ultrasound shows nodule size and suspicious features: hypoechogenicity, marked internal vascularity, irregular borders, height greater than width, irregular macrocalcifications, fine, stippled psammomatous microcalcifications (papillary thyroid carcinoma), dense homogenous irregular calcification (medullary thyroid carcinoma)
claims.quote: Ultrasound is useful in determining the size of the nodule and detecting suspicious sonographic characteristics including the following: Hypoechogenicity Marked internal vascularity Irregular borders Height of the nodule being greater than the width Irregular macrocalcifications Fine, stippled psammomatous microcalcifications (papillary thyroid carcinoma) Dense, homogenous irregular calcification (medullary thyroid carcinoma)

claims.text: TI-RADS: cancer risk stratification based largely on ultrasound (size, echogenicity, composition, shape, margins, echogenic foci); useful to decide when to do fine-needle aspiration
claims.quote: The thyroid imaging and reporting system (TI-RADS) is a risk stratification system for thyroid cancer based largely on ultrasound findings. A TI-RADS classification based on nodule size, echogenicity, composition, shape, margins, and echogenic foci is useful to decide when to proceed with a fine-needle aspiration biopsy (2).

claims.text: First test TSH: if low (hyperthyroidism) → radioiodine uptake and scan, and hot nodules are seldom malignant; if not hyperthyroid → thyroid ultrasound
claims.quote: Initial laboratory evaluation of a thyroid nodule consists of testing for: TSH If TSH is low (consistent with hyperthyroidism), radioiodine uptake and scanning are done. Nodules with increased radionuclide uptake (hot) are seldom malignant. If thyroid function tests do not indicate hyperthyroidism, the next step is to examine the nodule with thyroid ultrasound.

claims.text: Bethesda cytology: FNAB cells may distinguish benign (Bethesda II) from suspicious for malignancy (Bethesda V) or malignant (Bethesda VI); for indeterminate lesions (Bethesda III or IV), molecular analysis or calcitonin (possible medullary carcinoma) may add clarity
claims.quote: The Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology is another useful risk stratification tool. Cytologic examination of the cells obtained from FNAB may distinguish benign (Bethesda II) from suspicious for malignancy (Bethesda V) or malignant (Bethesda VI) lesions. For lesions that are cytologically indeterminate (Bethesda III or IV) (3), molecular analysis of the FNAB aspirate for mutations and rearrangements or measurement of calcitonin for possible medullary thyroid carcinoma may add sufficient diagnostic clarity to allow an optimally informed treatment recommendation.

claims.text: Causes Most nodules are benign: hyperplastic colloid goiter, thyroid cysts, thyroiditis, thyroid adenomas; malignant cause: thyroid cancers
claims.quote: Most nodules are benign. Benign causes include: Hyperplastic colloid goiter Thyroid cysts Thyroiditis Thyroid adenomas Malignant causes include: Thyroid cancers

claims.text: Palpation finds nodules in approximately 5% of middle-aged and older patients; ultrasound and autopsy studies suggest approximately 50% of older adults have them; many are found incidentally on head and neck imaging
claims.quote: In middle-aged and older patients, palpation reveals nodules in approximately 5%. Results of ultrasound and autopsy studies suggest that nodules are present in approximately 50% of older adults (1). Many nodules are found incidentally when head and neck imaging studies are done for other disorders.

claims.text: Thyroid cancer risk factors: thyroid irradiation, especially in infancy or childhood; age > 55; female sex; family history of thyroid cancer or MEN 2; a solitary nodule or goiter; dysphagia; dysphonia; increasing size; higher TSH
claims.quote: Risk factors for thyroid cancer include: History of thyroid irradiation, especially in infancy or childhood Age > 55 years Female sex (1) Family history of thyroid cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 A solitary nodule or goiter Dysphagia Dysphonia Increasing size (particularly rapid growth or growth while receiving thyroid suppression treatment) Higher thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels

claims.text: Symptoms Mostly asymptomatic, occasionally painful or compressive; pain suggests thyroiditis or hemorrhage into a cyst; an asymptomatic nodule may be malignant but is usually benign; compressive symptoms (difficulty swallowing or breathing, hoarseness) increase malignancy risk
claims.quote: Thyroid nodules are mostly asymptomatic, but they can occasionally be painful or cause compressive symptoms in the neck. Pain suggests thyroiditis or hemorrhage into a cyst. An asymptomatic nodule may be malignant but is usually benign. Compressive symptoms, including difficulty swallowing, difficulty breathing, or hoarseness, increase the risk of the nodule being malignant.

claims.text: Hyperthyroid symptoms suggest a hyperfunctioning adenoma or thyroiditis; hypothyroid symptoms suggest Hashimoto thyroiditis
claims.quote: Symptoms of hyperthyroidism (ie, palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremors) suggest a hyperfunctioning adenoma or thyroiditis, whereas symptoms of hypothyroidism (ie, cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue) suggest Hashimoto thyroiditis.

claims.text: Exam signs suggesting cancer: stony, hard consistency or fixation to surrounding structures, cervical lymphadenopathy, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis)
claims.quote: Signs that suggest thyroid cancer include stony, hard consistency or fixation to surrounding structures, cervical lymphadenopathy, and hoarseness (due to recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis).

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: FNA per TI-RADS criteria
claims.locator: Non-Trauma Ultrasound Findings, Vascular / Soft Tissue / Neck table

claims.text: Ultrasound-guided FNAB for nodules > 1 cm with suspicious features (TI-RADS 5) or > 1.5 cm with moderately suspicious features (TI-RADS 4); generally not recommended for nodules < 1 cm or entirely cystic nodules
claims.quote: For nodules > 1 cm with suspicious features (TI-RADS 5) or nodules > 1.5 cm with moderately suspicious features (TI-RADS 4), fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) done under ultrasound guidance is the procedure of choice to distinguish benign from malignant nodules. FNAB is generally not recommended for nodules < 1 cm or for nodules that are entirely cystic.

claims.text: Treatment is directed at the underlying disorder and depends on cytology; malignant nodules are treated as thyroid cancers
claims.quote: Treatment is directed at the underlying disorder and depends on cytology results (1). Treatment of malignant nodules is discussed under Thyroid Cancers.

claims.text: Benign nodules with Hashimoto thyroiditis or other hypothyroid goiter may stabilize or shrink with thyroxine replacement; TSH suppression for small benign nodules without hypothyroidism is seldom done; thyroxine is not used for cancerous nodules
claims.quote: Benign nodules in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis or other causes of goiter associated with hypothyroidism may stabilize or shrink with thyroxine replacement in doses that render the patient euthyroid. For small benign nodules (usually ≤ 1.5 cm) not associated with hypothyroidism, thyroxine suppression of TSH effectively shrinks the nodule in no more than half the cases, and is seldom done. Thyroxine is not used to treat cancerous nodules.

claims.text: Large compressive benign nodules can shrink after radiofrequency ablation; partial or complete thyroidectomy for nodules that continue to grow or compress; toxic nodules may be treated with radioactive iodine
claims.quote: Large benign nodules that compress the surrounding neck structures can shrink following radiofrequency ablation (2, 3). Partial or complete thyroidectomy is effective for treating nodules that continue to grow or cause compressive symptoms. Toxic (producing thyroid hormone and causing symptomatic hyperthyroidism) nodules may be treated with radioactive iodine to control hyperthyroidism and reduce nodule size.
